goals: Define price elasticity of demand and draw the five degrees
Calculate price elasticity by the percentage method and find an unknown price or quantity
Judge whether demand is elastic, unitary or inelastic from changes in total expenditure

slides.heading: Elasticity of Demand
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **how much** buyers respond to a price change, the **five degrees**, the **percentage method** and the **total expenditure method**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: meaning, five degrees, the percentage method, finding an unknown price or quantity, and the outlay method
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: The Law of Demand tells us the direction in which buyers react to a price change. But a shopkeeper also wants to know how much they react. Will a small price cut bring a flood of customers, or hardly any? That size of response is called elasticity of demand. In this part we define it, see its five degrees, and learn two ways to measure it.

slides.heading: What price elasticity measures
slides.body_md:
**Price elasticity of demand (Ed)** is the degree of responsiveness of the quantity demanded of a good to a change in **its own price**.

Ed = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price.

visual.alt: Flow: a change in the good's own price leads to a response in quantity demanded, and comparing the two percentage changes gives the elasticity
visual.caption: A ratio of two percentage changes

slides.narration: Elasticity compares two percentage changes: how much the quantity bought changes, against how much the price changed. Because both are percentages, the answer has no units. It does not matter whether we count rice in kilograms or quintals. A big number means buyers are very sensitive to price; a small number means they hardly react.

slides.narration: Three cases are special. If buyers will take any amount at one price but nothing at a slightly higher price, demand is perfectly elastic and the curve is horizontal. If they buy exactly the same amount whatever the price, demand is perfectly inelastic and the curve is vertical. If total spending never changes, demand is unitary elastic and the curve is a rectangular hyperbola.

slides.narration: Most real goods fall between the extremes. When quantity responds more than in proportion to price, demand is relatively elastic, and we draw a flatter curve. When quantity responds less than in proportion, demand is relatively inelastic, and we draw a steeper curve. Remember that comparing flat and steep only works where two curves pass through the same point.

slides.narration: Ask whether the quantity changes at all when the price changes. If it never changes, think about which line shows that.

One is the dividing line. Above one, buyers are sensitive; between zero and one, they are not very sensitive. Learn this table well: one-mark questions often test it.

slides.heading: The percentage (proportionate) method
slides.body_md:
**Ed = (ΔQ ÷ Q) ÷ (ΔP ÷ P) = (ΔQ ÷ ΔP) × (P ÷ Q)**

Q and P are the **original** quantity and price. The answer is negative because price and quantity move in opposite directions; we **drop the minus sign** and report Ed as a positive number.

nodes.label: Divide the first by the second

visual.alt: Flow of the percentage method: divide the change in quantity by the original quantity, divide the change in price by the original price, divide the first result by the second, drop the minus sign, and compare the answer with one
visual.caption: Percentage (proportionate) method, step by step

slides.narration: To measure elasticity exactly we use the percentage method. Find the change in quantity as a fraction of the original quantity, and the change in price as a fraction of the original price. Divide the first by the second. The result comes out negative for a normal good, so we drop the minus sign. Then compare the number with one.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: idli plates in Chennai
slides.body_md: An imagined tiffin centre cuts the idli price from ₹40 to ₹32; plates sold rise from 200 to 260.
bullets: Step 1 — Change in quantity as a share of 200.
Step 2 — Change in price as a share of 40.
Step 3 — Divide, drop the sign, compare with 1.

visual.alt: Worked example table for idli plates: quantity rises 30 per cent, price falls 20 per cent, elasticity is 1.5, so demand is relatively elastic
visual.caption: Imagined Chennai tiffin centre: price ₹40 to ₹32, plates 200 to 260.

slides.narration: Sales rise by sixty plates out of two hundred, which is thirty per cent. The price falls by eight rupees out of forty, which is twenty per cent. Thirty divided by twenty gives one point five. That is more than one, so demand for idli plates at this centre is relatively elastic.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: finding the new quantity
slides.body_md: An imagined Ahmedabad kite seller sells 500 kites a day at ₹50; Ed = 0.8. She raises the price to ₹55.
bullets: Step 1 — Percentage rise in price.
Step 2 — Multiply by Ed to get the percentage fall in quantity.
Step 3 — Subtract that share from 500.

visual.alt: Worked example table for kites: a 10 per cent price rise with elasticity 0.8 gives an 8 per cent fall in quantity, so daily sales fall from 500 to 460 kites
visual.caption: Imagined Ahmedabad kite seller before Uttarayan.

slides.narration: Sometimes we know the elasticity and must find the new quantity. The price rises by five rupees out of fifty, which is ten per cent. Elasticity is zero point eight, so quantity falls by eight per cent. Eight per cent of five hundred is forty kites, so she now sells four hundred and sixty kites a day.

slides.heading: Finding an unknown price
columns:
**Known:** Ed, the original price and the change in quantity.

**Step 1:** percentage change in quantity.

**Step 2:** divide by Ed to get the percentage change in price.

**Step 3:** apply that percentage to the original price.

**Check:** a price cut should go with a rise in quantity, and a price rise with a fall.

visual.alt: Small table for an imagined Kolkata sweet shop: the price of a rosogolla box falls 20 per cent and boxes sold rise 20 per cent, so elasticity is 1

slides.narration: We can also work backwards to a price. First find the percentage change in quantity. Divide it by the elasticity to get the percentage change in price, then apply it to the original price. The small table shows a sweet shop where a twenty per cent price cut brought a twenty per cent rise in boxes sold, so elasticity is exactly one.

slides.heading: Quick check: rosogolla boxes
slides.body_md: Price ₹200 → ₹160; boxes 150 → 180. What is the degree of elasticity?
slides.narration: Work out both percentage changes from the original values and compare them.

slides.heading: The total expenditure (outlay) method
slides.body_md:
Compare buyers' **total spending** on the good (price × quantity) before and after a price change.

- Spending moves **opposite** to price → **elastic**
- Spending **unchanged** → **unitary**
- Spending moves in the **same direction** as price → **inelastic**

visual.alt: Table for the total expenditure method: if spending moves opposite to price demand is elastic, if spending is unchanged it is unitary, and if spending moves in the same direction as price it is inelastic
visual.caption: Outlay method: read the direction of total spending, not exact values.

slides.narration: A second way to judge elasticity looks at how much buyers spend in total. If a price cut makes total spending rise, buyers responded strongly, so demand is elastic. If spending stays the same, demand is unitary. If spending falls with the price, demand is inelastic. This method tells us the degree, not an exact number.

slides.heading: The outlay test in one question

nodes.label: Did total spending move opposite to price?
Yes: elastic. Unchanged: unitary. Same direction: inelastic

visual.alt: Flow for the outlay method: when price changes, check whether total spending moved opposite to price (elastic), stayed the same (unitary) or moved in the same direction (inelastic)
visual.caption: The outlay test in one question

slides.narration: You can reduce the outlay method to one question. After the price changed, did total spending move the opposite way, stay the same, or move the same way? Opposite means elastic, unchanged means unitary, and the same way means inelastic.

slides.heading: Quick check: spending stays the same
slides.body_md: Readers spend the same total on a newspaper after its price changes. Their demand is…
slides.narration: Unchanged spending points to one particular degree. Which one?

slides.heading: Limits of the outlay method
slides.body_md:
- It shows only **three categories**, not the exact coefficient.
- It cannot separate perfectly elastic or perfectly inelastic cases from the others.
- In the ISC syllabus, numericals are set on the **percentage method** only.
slides.narration: The outlay method is quick and practical for a shopkeeper who watches her takings, but it has limits. It cannot tell us whether elasticity is one point two or three, only that it is above one. For exact values, and for every numerical question in your examination, use the percentage method.

slides.narration: Think of the insulin example and the vertical line.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Responsiveness of quantity demanded to own price
Infinite, zero, one, greater than one, between zero and one
Ed = (ΔQ ÷ Q) ÷ (ΔP ÷ P), initial values, sign dropped
Spending opposite to price: elastic; same direction: inelastic

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning of price elasticity, the five degrees, the percentage method and the total expenditure method

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Price elasticity measures how strongly quantity demanded responds to the good's own price. It has five degrees, from infinite to zero. The percentage method gives an exact value from the original price and quantity, with the minus sign dropped. The outlay method judges the degree from the direction of total spending.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always divide by the **original** price and quantity; write the formula first.
Drop the minus sign and **say so**; then state the degree (elastic, unitary or inelastic).
Numericals in the ISC paper are set on the **percentage method** only.
For the outlay method, write the **direction** of spending, then the conclusion.
2 marks: formula and answer; 3 marks: working, answer and the degree with a reason.
slides.narration: A few habits earn marks. Write the formula before substituting. Divide by the original values, and state clearly that you have dropped the minus sign. Always finish a numerical by naming the degree of elasticity. In outlay method questions, say which way spending moved before you give your conclusion.

slides.narration: On a straight-line demand curve, pick a point and split the line there. The lower segment runs from the point down to the quantity axis; the upper segment runs up to the price axis. Elasticity at the point is the lower segment divided by the upper one. At the mid-point they are equal, so elasticity is one.

slides.narration: As we slide down the line the lower segment shrinks and the upper segment grows. So elasticity falls from infinity where the line touches the price axis, through values above one, to exactly one at the mid-point, then below one, and finally zero at the quantity axis. A straight line does not have the same elasticity everywhere.

slides.narration: If the demand curve is curved, draw a tangent that just touches it at the point and extend the tangent to both axes. Elasticity at the point is the lower part of the tangent divided by the upper part. The idea is the same as for a straight line, applied to the tangent.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading elasticity off a line
slides.body_md: A straight demand line for gym memberships in an imagined Pune suburb meets both axes. Describe Ed at the top end, above the middle, at the middle, below it and at the bottom end.
bullets: Step 1 — Write Ed = lower ÷ upper.
Step 2 — Compare the two segments at each position.
Step 3 — State the degree at each position.

visual.alt: Table of elasticity at five positions on a straight-line demand curve: infinite at the price axis, greater than one above the mid-point, one at the mid-point, less than one below it, and zero at the quantity axis

slides.narration: Let us reason it out. At the top end the upper segment is zero, so elasticity is infinite. Above the middle the lower segment is longer, so elasticity is more than one. In the middle they match, so it is one. Below the middle it is less than one, and at the bottom end the lower segment vanishes, so elasticity is zero.

slides.heading: What makes demand elastic or inelastic?

rows: It takes a large share of income

visual.alt: Table of seven factors affecting price elasticity: substitutes, nature of the good, share of income, number of uses, postponement, time period and habit, with when each makes demand more elastic and an imagined example

slides.narration: Why are some goods elastic and others not? Close substitutes, luxury status, a large share of income, many uses, purchases that can be postponed and a long time to adjust all make demand more elastic. Necessities, tiny budget shares, urgent purchases and habits make it less elastic.

slides.heading: Price level and habit
columns: **Very cheap goods** (a pencil) and **very costly goods** bought by the rich (a luxury car) both have **inelastic** demand: price changes hardly affect these buyers.
**Habit-forming goods** (a daily cup of tea) keep being bought after a price rise, so their demand is **inelastic**.

rows: Rich buyers barely notice the price

visual.alt: Small table: a pencil, a luxury car and daily tea all have inelastic demand, because of a tiny budget share, rich buyers and habit respectively

slides.narration: Two more factors are worth noting. Goods at the very bottom or the very top of the price range tend to have inelastic demand, because buyers either do not notice the cost or can easily afford it. Habits, like a morning cup of tea, also keep demand steady when prices rise.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: biscuits versus wheat flour
slides.body_md: Compare the elasticity of demand for one brand of biscuits and for wheat flour, for families in an imagined Indore market.
bullets: Step 1 — Check substitutes.
Step 2 — Check the nature of the good.
Step 3 — Check postponement, then conclude.

visual.alt: Worked example table comparing one brand of biscuits with wheat flour: biscuits have many substitutes, are a snack and can be postponed, so demand is elastic; flour has few substitutes, is a necessity and cannot be postponed, so demand is inelastic

slides.narration: Take each factor in turn. One biscuit brand has many rivals on the shelf, it is a snack and it can be skipped, so its demand is elastic. Wheat flour has few close substitutes, it is a daily necessity and buying cannot wait, so its demand is inelastic. Three reasons, one clear conclusion.

slides.heading: Quick check: goods with many uses
slides.body_md: Electricity is used for lighting, cooking, water pumps and workshops. Its demand tends to be…
slides.narration: If a good can move into more uses when it is cheaper, how strongly does its demand respond?

slides.heading: Time makes demand more elastic

nodes.label: Short run: few choices, demand inelastic
Over time: metro, e-scooters, car pools

visual.alt: Flow showing that when petrol becomes dearer, demand is inelastic in the short run but becomes more elastic in the long run as buyers adopt the metro, electric scooters and car pools
visual.caption: Time makes demand more elastic

slides.narration: Time matters a great deal. When petrol becomes dearer, most commuters cannot change their travel at once, so demand is inelastic. Over months and years they take the metro, buy electric scooters or share cars. In the long run demand becomes more elastic.

slides.heading: Income elasticity of demand
slides.body_md: **Income elasticity** = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in income.

rows: Inferior good: bought less as income rises
Demand does not change with income

visual.alt: Table of income elasticity: negative for inferior goods, zero when income has no effect, between zero and one for necessities, and above one for luxuries, with imagined examples

slides.narration: Income elasticity measures how demand responds to a change in income rather than price. Its sign matters. A negative value marks an inferior good, bought less as people get richer. A value between zero and one marks a necessity, and a value above one marks a luxury, whose demand grows faster than income.

slides.heading: Quick check: packaged juice
slides.body_md: Families buy more packaged juice as incomes rise. Income elasticity is…
slides.narration: Do quantity and income move in the same direction or opposite directions?

slides.heading: Cross elasticity of demand
slides.body_md: **Cross elasticity** = percentage change in quantity of X ÷ percentage change in the price of Y.

visual.alt: Table of cross elasticity: substitutes such as tea and coffee have a positive sign, complements such as cars and petrol a negative sign, and unrelated goods zero

slides.narration: Cross elasticity measures how demand for one good responds to the price of another. If a dearer coffee makes people buy more tea, the sign is positive and the goods are substitutes. If dearer petrol makes people buy fewer cars, the sign is negative and they are complements. Unrelated goods give zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: three kinds of elasticity
slides.body_md: Match each response to the right elasticity.
bullets: Own price changes → price elasticity.
Income changes → income elasticity.
A related good's price changes → cross elasticity.

rows: % change in quantity ÷ % change in own price
% change in quantity ÷ % change in income
% change in quantity of X ÷ % change in price of Y

visual.alt: Table comparing price, income and cross elasticity: what each responds to and its formula in words

slides.narration: All three elasticities share one pattern: a percentage change in quantity divided by a percentage change in something else. Ask what changed. If it is the good's own price, use price elasticity. If it is income, use income elasticity. If it is the price of another good, use cross elasticity.

slides.heading: Quick check: cabs and autos
slides.body_md: Dearer cab fares lead to more auto-rickshaw rides. The cross elasticity is…
slides.narration: Do the cab fare and auto rides move together or in opposite directions?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Lower segment ÷ upper segment; tangent for a curve
Substitutes, nature, income share, uses, postponement, time, habit
Negative: inferior; 0 to 1: necessity; above 1: luxury
Positive: substitutes; negative: complements; zero: unrelated

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: the point method, the factors affecting elasticity, income elasticity and cross elasticity

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. The point method divides the lower segment by the upper segment, using a tangent for curves, so elasticity changes along a straight line. Substitutes, the nature of the good, income share, uses, postponement, time and habit decide how elastic demand is. Income and cross elasticity are read mainly from their signs.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Point method: **lower ÷ upper**; mid-point gives Ed = 1. No numericals on this method in ISC.
For a factor question, name the factor, give its **direction** and an **example**.
Income elasticity: **negative = inferior**, **0 to 1 = necessity**, **above 1 = luxury**.
Cross elasticity: **positive = substitutes**, **negative = complements**, **zero = unrelated**.
In comparisons, end with a clear conclusion: which good is more elastic and why.
slides.narration: For the point method, remember lower over upper and that the mid-point gives one. For factor questions, always name the factor, say which way it pushes elasticity, and add an example. For income and cross elasticity, the sign is the key: learn the three meanings of each sign.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and degrees of price elasticity
sections.body_md:
**Price elasticity of demand** is the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the good's **own price**. It is a ratio of two percentage changes, so it has **no units**.

| Degree | Ed | Curve |
|---|---|---|
| Perfectly elastic | ∞ | Horizontal |
| Perfectly inelastic | 0 | Vertical |
| Unitary | 1 | Rectangular hyperbola |
| Relatively elastic | > 1 | Flatter |
| Relatively inelastic | between 0 and 1 | Steeper |

Flat-versus-steep comparisons are valid only **at a common point**, because Ed also depends on P ÷ Q.

sections.heading: 2. The percentage (proportionate) method
sections.body_md:
**Ed = (ΔQ ÷ Q) ÷ (ΔP ÷ P) = (ΔQ ÷ ΔP) × (P ÷ Q)**, where Q and P are the **original** values. The ratio is negative for a normal demand curve; by convention the **minus sign is dropped**.

**Unknown quantity:** percentage change in quantity = Ed × percentage change in price.
**Unknown price:** percentage change in price = percentage change in quantity ÷ Ed.

In ISC 2027, **all numericals** on price elasticity use this method.

key_terms.definition_md: Another name for the percentage method, using changes divided by original values.

sections.heading: 5. Factors affecting price elasticity
sections.body_md:
- **Substitutes:** more and closer substitutes → more elastic.
- **Nature:** necessities inelastic, luxuries elastic.
- **Share of income:** tiny share → inelastic.
- **Number of uses:** many uses → more elastic.
- **Postponement:** purchases that can wait → elastic.
- **Time period:** more elastic in the long run.
- **Habits** and **price level** (very cheap or very costly goods) → inelastic.

sections.heading: 6. Income and cross elasticity
sections.body_md:
**Income elasticity** = % change in quantity ÷ % change in income: **negative** for inferior goods, **0 to 1** for necessities, **above 1** for luxuries.

**Cross elasticity** = % change in quantity of X ÷ % change in price of Y: **positive** for substitutes, **negative** for complements, **zero** for unrelated goods.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Dividing by the **new** price or quantity instead of the original values.
- Forgetting to drop the minus sign, or dropping it without saying so.
- Calling a flatter curve more elastic without noting that the comparison holds at a common point.
- Attempting numericals on the outlay or point method (ISC sets them on the percentage method only).
- Mixing up signs: substitutes have a positive cross elasticity, complements a negative one.

questions.stem_md: Price elasticity of demand for a good measures

options.text_md: how strongly the price responds to a change in the quantity supplied
how strongly the quantity demanded responds to a change in the good's own price
the change in demand caused by a change in consumers' income
the total amount buyers spend on the good in a year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** how strongly the quantity demanded responds to a change in the good's own price. It is the degree of responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the good's own price. Income responses are income elasticity; spending totals and supply responses are different ideas.

questions.stem_md: A government milk booth in an imagined Bhubaneswar ward sells any quantity at a fixed ₹54 a litre, and at even a paisa more nobody buys from it. The demand curve facing the booth is

options.text_md: a vertical straight line (perfectly inelastic)
a rectangular hyperbola (unitary elastic)
a steep downward line (relatively inelastic)
a horizontal straight line (perfectly elastic)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a horizontal straight line (perfectly elastic). Any quantity is bought at one price and none at a slightly higher price: elasticity is infinite and the demand curve is horizontal. A vertical line would mean quantity never changes.

questions.stem_md: A patient in an imagined Bhopal hospital needs exactly 30 insulin vials a month whatever their price. Her demand curve for insulin is best drawn as

options.text_md: a vertical line at 30 vials
a horizontal line at the current price
a curve on which price × quantity is constant
a gently sloping downward line

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a vertical line at 30 vials. Quantity does not change at all when price changes, so Ed = 0 and the curve is vertical at 30 vials.

questions.stem_md: On a demand curve that has unitary elasticity at every point, the product of price and quantity

options.text_md: doubles whenever the price is halved
is zero where the curve meets the price axis
stays the same at every point, so the curve is a rectangular hyperbola
rises as we move down the curve

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** stays the same at every point, so the curve is a rectangular hyperbola. With Ed = 1 everywhere, a given percentage fall in price is matched by an equal percentage rise in quantity, so spending P × Q is constant: the curve is a rectangular hyperbola.

questions.stem_md: Two straight demand curves for paper kites in an imagined Ahmedabad pol pass through the same point. Curve K is much flatter than curve M. At that common point,

options.text_md: demand on M is more elastic than on K
both have unitary elasticity
demand on K is more elastic than on M
elasticity cannot be compared at a common point

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** demand on K is more elastic than on M. Through a common point, Ed = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q) has the same P/Q, so the flatter curve (larger ΔQ for a given ΔP) is more elastic.

questions.stem_md: Demand is called relatively elastic when

options.text_md: the percentage change in quantity demanded is greater than the percentage change in price
quantity demanded does not change at all when price changes
the percentage changes in quantity and price are equal
quantity demanded becomes infinite at a given price

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the percentage change in quantity demanded is greater than the percentage change in price. Relatively elastic means Ed > 1: quantity responds more than in proportion to price. The other options describe Ed = 0, Ed = 1 and Ed = ∞.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Price elasticity of demand is a pure number, so the elasticity for rice in kilograms is the same as in quintals.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** It compares two percentage changes, so the units cancel; measuring rice in kilograms or quintals leaves the coefficient unchanged.

questions.stem_md: When quantity demanded does not change at all as price changes, demand is perfectly ___ and the coefficient of elasticity is ___.
questions.solution_md: An unchanged quantity means demand is perfectly inelastic with a coefficient of zero (0).

questions.stem_md: Match each value of the price elasticity coefficient with the shape of the demand curve that shows it.

options.text_md: Ed = 0
Ed = ∞
Ed = 1 at every point
Ed greater than 1 through a point

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Zero response gives a vertical line, infinite response a horizontal line, constant spending a rectangular hyperbola, and a strong response a flatter curve.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Two demand curves drawn through the same point can have different elasticities at that point.

**Reason (R):** Price elasticity of demand depends only on the slope of the demand curve.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: through a common point the flatter curve is more elastic. R is false: elasticity depends on the slope and on the ratio P/Q (Ed = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q)), not on slope alone.

questions.stem_md: Name the five degrees of price elasticity of demand and state the value or range of the coefficient for each.
questions.solution_md: Five names, each with its coefficient.

answer.model_answer_md: 1. **Perfectly elastic:** Ed = ∞. 2. **Perfectly inelastic:** Ed = 0. 3. **Unitary elastic:** Ed = 1. 4. **Relatively elastic:** Ed > 1. 5. **Relatively inelastic:** Ed lies between 0 and 1.

questions.stem_md: A family in an imagined Kolkata neighbourhood always spends exactly ₹600 a month on sweets, whatever their price. What is its price elasticity of demand for sweets? Explain.
questions.solution_md: Constant outlay implies Ed = 1.

answer.model_answer_md: The family keeps **total spending constant**, so any percentage rise in price is matched by an equal percentage fall in quantity. Its demand is **unitary elastic (Ed = 1)**, and its demand curve is a **rectangular hyperbola**.

marking_scheme.step: Constant spending linked to equal percentage changes

questions.stem_md: Rohan says, "A flatter demand curve is always more elastic than a steeper one." Comment on his statement with reference to two straight-line demand curves for bus passes in an imagined Nagpur depot.
questions.solution_md: Correct at a common point; not in general, because elasticity also depends on P/Q.

answer.model_answer_md: Rohan is right only **at a common point**. Ed = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q): where two lines cross, **P/Q is the same**, so the **flatter** line (larger ΔQ for each rupee) has the higher elasticity. But **at different points** the P/Q ratios differ, so a flatter line at a low price can be **less elastic** than a steeper line at a high price. Slope alone does not decide elasticity.

marking_scheme.step: Not true in general, with reason

questions.stem_md: Describe the diagrams of perfectly elastic, perfectly inelastic and unitary elastic demand, naming the axes and the shape of each curve.
questions.solution_md: Axes plus three shapes.

answer.model_answer_md: In each diagram **quantity** is on the x-axis and **price** on the y-axis. **Perfectly elastic:** a **horizontal line** at one price; any quantity is sold there. **Perfectly inelastic:** a **vertical line** at one quantity; it does not change with price. **Unitary elastic:** a **rectangular hyperbola**, where price times quantity is the same at every point.

questions.stem_md: Explain the five degrees of price elasticity of demand, describing the demand curve for each, and give an imagined Indian example of a good that might show each degree.
questions.solution_md: Five degrees, each with value, curve and example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Perfectly elastic (Ed = ∞):** a **horizontal** curve; any quantity at one price — a government booth selling milk at a fixed price.
2. **Perfectly inelastic (Ed = 0):** a **vertical** curve — insulin for a diabetic patient.
3. **Unitary elastic (Ed = 1):** a **rectangular hyperbola**; spending stays the same — a family with a fixed sweets budget.
4. **Relatively elastic (Ed > 1):** a **flatter** curve; quantity responds strongly — restaurant meals or branded clothes.
5. **Relatively inelastic (Ed between 0 and 1):** a **steeper** curve; quantity responds weakly — salt or matchboxes.

marking_scheme.step: Perfectly elastic with curve and example
Perfectly inelastic with curve and example
Relatively elastic with curve and example
Relatively inelastic with curve and example

questions.stem_md: An imagined Chennai tiffin centre cuts the price of an idli plate from ₹40 to ₹32, and morning sales rise from 200 to 260 plates. Calculate the price elasticity of demand by the percentage method.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Percentage change in quantity = (260 − 200) ÷ 200 × 100 = 30.
Step 2: Percentage change in price = (32 − 40) ÷ 40 × 100 = -20.
Step 3: Ed = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5 (minus sign dropped). Demand is relatively elastic.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined Ahmedabad pol a kite seller sells 500 kites a day at ₹50 each. Her price elasticity of demand is 0.8. How many kites a day will she sell if she raises the price to ₹55?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Percentage rise in price = 5 ÷ 50 × 100 = 10.
Step 2: Percentage fall in quantity = 0.8 × 10 = 8.
Step 3: New quantity = 500 − 8 per cent of 500 = 500 − 40 = 460 kites.

marking_scheme.step: Percentage change in price and quantity

questions.stem_md: A tender-coconut seller on an imagined Goa beach sells 400 coconuts a day at ₹30 each. Her price elasticity of demand is 2. To what price must she cut her coconuts to sell 480 a day?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Percentage rise in quantity = 80 ÷ 400 × 100 = 20.
Step 2: Required percentage fall in price = 20 ÷ 2 = 10.
Step 3: New price = 30 − 10 per cent of 30 = ₹27.

marking_scheme.step: Percentage change in quantity and required price change

questions.stem_md: An imagined Ludhiana dairy raised the price of paneer from ₹80 a kg, and daily sales fell from 250 kg to 235 kg. If its price elasticity of demand is 0.6, what is the new price of paneer?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Percentage fall in quantity = 15 ÷ 250 × 100 = 6.
Step 2: Percentage rise in price = 6 ÷ 0.6 = 10.
Step 3: New price = 80 + 10 per cent of 80 = ₹88.

questions.stem_md: The price elasticity of demand for tickets at an imagined Indore multiplex is 1.25. By what percentage will the number of tickets sold rise if the multiplex cuts its ticket price by 8 per cent?
questions.solution_md: Percentage change in quantity = Ed × percentage change in price = 1.25 × 8 = 10 per cent rise.

questions.stem_md: A kirana store in an imagined Kanpur market raises iodised salt from ₹20 to ₹25 a kg, and its weekly sales fall from 400 kg to 380 kg. The price elasticity of demand for salt here is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 0.2. Quantity falls 20 ÷ 400 = 5 per cent; price rises 5 ÷ 20 = 25 per cent; Ed = 5 ÷ 25 = 0.2 (relatively inelastic). 5 inverts the ratio; 0.25 and 1.25 use wrong bases.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Kolkata sweet shop cuts the price of a rosogolla box from ₹200 to ₹160, and sales rise from 150 to 180 boxes a day. Demand for the boxes is

options.text_md: relatively elastic
unitary elastic
relatively inelastic
perfectly elastic

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** unitary elastic. Price falls 40 ÷ 200 = 20 per cent and quantity rises 30 ÷ 150 = 20 per cent, so Ed = 1: unitary elastic.

questions.stem_md: Auto-rickshaw drivers in an imagined Jaipur colony raise the fare from ₹60 to ₹66 a ride, and weekly rides fall from 1,200 to 1,020. The price elasticity of demand for these rides is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 1.5. Quantity falls 180 ÷ 1200 = 15 per cent; price rises 6 ÷ 60 = 10 per cent; Ed = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5, relatively elastic. 0.67 inverts the ratio and 15 forgets to divide.

questions.stem_md: In the ISC percentage (proportionate) method used in this chapter, the percentage changes in price and quantity are calculated from

options.text_md: the new price and quantity
the initial (original) price and quantity
the average of the old and new values
the highest price on the demand schedule

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the initial (original) price and quantity. The proportionate method divides each change by its original value: ΔQ/Q and ΔP/P with Q and P the initial values.

questions.stem_md: A chemist in an imagined Bhopal market raises the price of a vial of insulin from ₹300 to ₹360; a regular patient still buys 30 vials a month. Her price elasticity of demand is

options.text_md: infinite

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 0. The quantity does not change, so the percentage change in quantity is zero and Ed = 0 (perfectly inelastic) whatever the price change.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The price elasticity coefficient worked out from a normal demand schedule comes out negative before its sign is dropped.

**Reason (R):** Price and quantity demanded change in opposite directions along a normal demand curve.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A: because price and quantity move in opposite directions, the ratio of their percentage changes is negative; by convention the minus sign is dropped and Ed is reported as a positive number.

questions.stem_md: Write the formula for price elasticity of demand by the percentage method and explain each symbol in it.
questions.solution_md: Formula with symbols defined.

answer.model_answer_md: **Ed = (ΔQ ÷ Q) ÷ (ΔP ÷ P) = (ΔQ ÷ ΔP) × (P ÷ Q)**, where **ΔQ** is the change in quantity demanded, **Q** the original quantity, **ΔP** the change in price and **P** the original price.

questions.stem_md: A stationery shop in an imagined Patna lane sells 600 notebooks a week at ₹40. The price elasticity of demand is 0.5. Find the weekly sales if the price rises to ₹50.
questions.solution_md: Percentage price change, percentage quantity change, new quantity.

answer.model_answer_md: Price rises **10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25 per cent**. Quantity falls **0.5 × 25 = 12.5 per cent**, that is 75 notebooks. New sales = **600 − 75 = 525 notebooks** a week.

questions.stem_md: The auto-rickshaw union of an imagined Jaipur colony raised fares from ₹60 to ₹66, and weekly rides fell from 1,200 to 1,020. Calculate the price elasticity of demand and judge whether the fare rise was wise for the drivers' total earnings.
questions.solution_md: Compute Ed, classify, and link elasticity to total earnings.

answer.model_answer_md: Quantity falls **180 ÷ 1200 = 15 per cent**; price rises **6 ÷ 60 = 10 per cent**; **Ed = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5**, so demand is **relatively elastic**. When demand is elastic, a **higher fare lowers total earnings**, because the proportionate fall in rides outweighs the higher fare per ride. The rise was **not wise** for the drivers.

questions.stem_md: A mobile store in an imagined Shillong market finds that the price elasticity of demand for its data packs is 3. It cuts the price of a pack by 5 per cent. By what percentage will sales rise, and what does this tell the store about its pricing?
questions.solution_md: Percentage change in quantity and its pricing meaning.

answer.model_answer_md: Percentage rise in sales = **Ed × percentage fall in price = 3 × 5 = 15 per cent**. Demand is **highly elastic**: a small price cut brings a much larger rise in sales, so **total spending on its packs rises**. The store gains customers and revenue by keeping its prices **low**, as long as its costs allow.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [2 + 3]

(a) An imagined Chennai tiffin centre cuts the price of an idli plate from ₹40 to ₹32, and sales rise from 200 to 260 plates a morning. Calculate the price elasticity of demand.
(b) A tender-coconut seller in an imagined Goa beach sells 400 coconuts a day at ₹30; her Ed is 2. Find the price at which she will sell 480 a day, and state whether her takings are likely to rise.
questions.solution_md: Percentage method in (a); unknown price and takings in (b).

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Quantity rises **60 ÷ 200 = 30 per cent**; price falls **8 ÷ 40 = 20 per cent**; **Ed = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5** (minus sign dropped), so demand is **relatively elastic**.
(b) Quantity must rise **80 ÷ 400 = 20 per cent**. With Ed = 2, the price must fall **20 ÷ 2 = 10 per cent**, so the new price is **₹27**. As demand is **elastic**, the proportionate rise in sales exceeds the fall in price, so her **takings rise**.

questions.stem_md: Under the total expenditure method, demand for a good is elastic (Ed > 1) when

options.text_md: total spending stays the same whatever the price
a fall in price lowers total spending on it
total spending moves in the same direction as price
a fall in price raises total spending on it and a rise in price lowers it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a fall in price raises total spending on it and a rise in price lowers it. With elastic demand quantity changes proportionately more than price, so spending moves opposite to price. Unchanged spending means unitary; spending moving with price means inelastic.

questions.stem_md: After a cooking-gas cylinder became dearer, households in an imagined Kanpur colony bought slightly fewer refills, yet their total spending on gas rose. Using the outlay method, their demand for gas is

options.text_md: relatively elastic
unitary elastic
perfectly elastic
relatively inelastic

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** relatively inelastic. Price rose and total spending also rose (same direction), so quantity fell proportionately less than price: demand is relatively inelastic.

questions.stem_md: Readers of an imagined Mysuru newspaper spend the same total amount on it before and after its cover price changes. By the outlay method, their demand is

options.text_md: perfectly elastic
perfectly inelastic
unitary elastic
relatively elastic

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** unitary elastic. Unchanged total spending when price changes indicates Ed = 1.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The total expenditure method gives the exact numerical value of price elasticity, such as 1.6 or 0.4.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. It only tells whether demand is elastic, unitary or inelastic, from the direction of change in spending; it cannot give an exact coefficient.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If the price of a good falls and buyers' total expenditure on it also falls, demand is relatively inelastic.

**Reason (R):** With inelastic demand, the percentage rise in quantity is smaller than the percentage fall in price.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A: the small rise in quantity cannot make up for the lower price, so spending falls with price, which marks inelastic demand.

questions.stem_md: State how total expenditure changes when price falls in each of the three cases of the outlay method: elastic, unitary and inelastic demand.
questions.solution_md: Three cases with direction of spending.

answer.model_answer_md: When price **falls**: with **elastic** demand total expenditure **rises**; with **unitary** demand it **stays the same**; with **inelastic** demand it **falls**. (A price rise reverses the first and last results.)

questions.stem_md: A textile shop in an imagined Surat market cut the prices of its sarees during a sale. The owner noticed that the money customers spent on sarees went up sharply. What can he conclude about the elasticity of demand, and should he repeat the sale for this good? Explain using the outlay method.
questions.solution_md: Opposite movement implies elastic; implication for revenue.

answer.model_answer_md: Price **fell** and total spending **rose**: spending moved **opposite** to price, so by the outlay method demand for his sarees is **elastic (Ed > 1)**. Buyers responded with a proportionately larger rise in purchases. A repeat sale should again **raise his revenue**, provided the extra sarees do not cost him more than they bring in.

questions.stem_md: By the point (geometric) method, price elasticity of demand at a point on a straight-line demand curve is equal to

options.text_md: the upper segment divided by the lower segment
the lower segment divided by the upper segment
the slope of the line multiplied by the price
the length of the whole line

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the lower segment divided by the upper segment. Ed at a point = lower segment (from the point to the quantity axis) ÷ upper segment (from the point to the price axis).

questions.stem_md: On a straight-line demand curve that meets both axes, elasticity equals one at

options.text_md: the mid-point of the line
the point where it meets the price axis
the point where it meets the quantity axis
every point, because the line is straight

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the mid-point of the line. At the mid-point the lower and upper segments are equal, so Ed = 1. At the price axis Ed is infinite; at the quantity axis it is zero.

questions.stem_md: A point lies on the upper half of a straight-line demand curve for gym memberships in an imagined Pune suburb, closer to the price axis. At that point demand is

options.text_md: relatively inelastic, because the lower segment is shorter
relatively elastic, because the lower segment is longer than the upper segment
unitary elastic, because the line is straight
perfectly inelastic, because the price is high

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** relatively elastic, because the lower segment is longer than the upper segment. Above the mid-point the lower segment exceeds the upper one, so their ratio is greater than 1: relatively elastic.

questions.stem_md: On a straight-line demand curve, elasticity is ___ at the point where the line meets the price axis and ___ where it meets the quantity axis.
questions.solution_md: At the price axis the upper segment is zero, so Ed is infinite; at the quantity axis the lower segment is zero, so Ed is zero (0).

questions.stem_md: Explain why elasticity is different at different points of the same straight-line demand curve.
questions.solution_md: Constant slope but changing P/Q, so changing segment ratio.

answer.model_answer_md: On a straight line the **slope is constant**, but **P ÷ Q changes**: high at the top, low at the bottom. So the **lower-to-upper segment ratio** falls down the line, from very elastic near the price axis to very inelastic near the quantity axis.

marking_scheme.step: Segment ratio falls down the line

questions.stem_md: A straight-line demand curve for cycle repairs in an imagined Ludhiana market meets both axes. Using the point method, describe the elasticity at five positions on it: at the price axis, above the mid-point, at the mid-point, below the mid-point and at the quantity axis.
questions.solution_md: Five positions with reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: With **Ed = lower segment ÷ upper segment**: at the **price axis** the upper segment is zero, so **Ed = ∞**; **above the mid-point** the lower segment is longer, so **Ed > 1**; at the **mid-point** the segments are equal, so **Ed = 1**; **below the mid-point** **Ed < 1**; at the **quantity axis** the lower segment is zero, so **Ed = 0**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [2 + 3]

(a) Explain the point (geometric) method of measuring price elasticity of demand on a straight-line demand curve.
(b) For a non-linear (curved) demand curve, explain how elasticity at a point is found, and show that a straight line cannot have the same elasticity at every point.
questions.solution_md: Segment ratio on a line; tangent for a curve; changing ratio along a line.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Take a point on the line and split the line there. Elasticity at the point is the **lower segment** (from the point to the quantity axis) **divided by the upper segment** (from the point to the price axis). At the mid-point the two are equal, so Ed = 1.
(b) For a curve, draw a **tangent** at the point and extend it to both axes; elasticity is the **lower segment of the tangent divided by its upper segment**. A straight line has a constant slope, but **P ÷ Q falls** as we move down it, so the segment ratio falls from **infinity at the price axis** to **zero at the quantity axis**. Only a **rectangular hyperbola** keeps Ed = 1 everywhere.

questions.stem_md: Demand for one brand of bathing soap in an imagined Coimbatore supermarket is highly elastic mainly because

options.text_md: soap takes a large share of a family's income
soap has only one use
buyers cannot postpone buying soap
many close substitutes are available on the same shelf

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** many close substitutes are available on the same shelf. A single brand faces many close substitutes, so a small price rise sends buyers to other brands. A small budget share and urgency would make demand less elastic.

questions.stem_md: A family in an imagined Varanasi colony hardly changes its purchase of matchboxes when their price rises by half. The best explanation is that

options.text_md: matchboxes take a tiny share of the family's income
matchboxes have many substitutes
matchboxes are a luxury
the family expects their price to fall

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** matchboxes take a tiny share of the family's income. Goods on which only a tiny part of income is spent have inelastic demand: even a large percentage price rise barely affects the budget.

questions.stem_md: When petrol prices rose, commuters in an imagined Hyderabad suburb first kept driving as before, but over the next two years many shifted to the metro and electric scooters. This shows that demand for petrol is

options.text_md: more elastic in the short run than in the long run
perfectly inelastic in both periods
more elastic in the long run than in the short run
unaffected by the availability of substitutes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** more elastic in the long run than in the short run. Over time buyers find and adopt substitutes and change habits, so demand becomes more elastic in the long run.

questions.stem_md: Electricity in an imagined Nashik town is used for lighting, cooking, pumping water and running workshops. Compared with a good that has a single use, its demand tends to be

options.text_md: perfectly inelastic, because it is essential
less elastic, because it has many uses
more elastic, because a fall in price lets it spread into more uses
unrelated to its number of uses

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** more elastic, because a fall in price lets it spread into more uses. A good with many uses can be switched into or out of several of them as its price changes, so its demand tends to be more elastic.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Demand for necessities such as salt is usually more elastic than demand for luxuries such as air-conditioned holidays.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Necessities have inelastic demand because they must be bought; luxuries can be postponed or dropped, so their demand is more elastic.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A lifelong tea drinker in an imagined Darjeeling town keeps buying the same amount of tea after its price rises.

**Reason (R):** Demand for goods consumed out of habit tends to be inelastic.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A: tea is part of his daily routine, a habit, so he does not cut back when its price rises; habit-forming goods have inelastic demand.

questions.stem_md: How do the nature of a good and the possibility of postponing its purchase affect its price elasticity of demand?
questions.solution_md: Two factors with direction and example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Nature:** necessities (rice, medicines) have **inelastic** demand, while luxuries (jewellery, foreign trips) have **elastic** demand. **Postponement:** if buying can be **delayed**, as with a new sofa, demand is **elastic**; if it is **urgent**, as with medicine, it is **inelastic**.

questions.stem_md: Why is the demand for very cheap goods, such as a pencil, and very costly goods, such as a luxury car, both relatively inelastic for the buyers in an imagined Delhi colony?
questions.solution_md: Price level and the buyers' income.

answer.model_answer_md: **Very cheap goods** take a negligible part of income, so price changes hardly matter. **Very costly goods** are bought by **rich buyers** for whom a price change makes little difference. Elasticity is highest for **medium-priced goods** bought by middle-income families.

questions.stem_md: Compare the likely price elasticity of demand for (a) a particular brand of biscuits and (b) wheat flour, for families in an imagined Indore market, giving three reasons.
questions.solution_md: Conclusion plus three reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: Demand for **one brand of biscuits** is **elastic**, while demand for **wheat flour** is **inelastic**. **Substitutes:** many other biscuit brands exist; staple flour has few close substitutes. **Nature:** biscuits are a snack that can be skipped; flour is a **necessity**. **Postponement:** biscuit purchases can be **delayed**, but families cannot postpone buying flour for daily rotis.

questions.stem_md: A state electricity board in an imagined hill state plans to raise power tariffs and claims that "demand will hardly fall". Evaluate this claim for the short run and the long run.
questions.solution_md: Short-run inelastic, long-run more elastic, with judgement.

answer.model_answer_md: In the **short run** the claim is largely **correct**: homes and workshops depend on electricity and cannot quickly change appliances, so demand is **inelastic**. In the **long run** it is **weaker**: users install **solar panels**, buy **energy-efficient** appliances and change habits, so demand becomes **more elastic** and consumption falls more. The board should not assume today's response will last.

marking_scheme.step: Long run: more elastic, with reason

questions.stem_md: Explain any five factors that affect the price elasticity of demand for a good, illustrating each with an imagined Indian example.
questions.solution_md: Five factors, each with direction and example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Availability of substitutes:** close substitutes make demand **elastic** — one brand of toothpaste.
2. **Nature of the good:** necessities are **inelastic** (salt), luxuries **elastic** (designer watches).
3. **Share of income spent:** a tiny share gives **inelastic** demand (matchboxes); a large share gives **elastic** demand (a new refrigerator).
4. **Number of uses:** goods with many uses, such as **electricity**, have more **elastic** demand.
5. **Time period:** demand is more **elastic in the long run**, when buyers find substitutes — commuters switching from petrol scooters to the metro.

questions.stem_md: Families in an imagined Kochi suburb buy more packaged juice as their incomes rise. The income elasticity of demand for packaged juice is

options.text_md: positive, so juice is a normal good for them
negative, so juice is an inferior good for them
zero, so income has no effect
infinite, because juice is a luxury

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** positive, so juice is a normal good for them. Quantity moves in the same direction as income, so income elasticity is positive: a normal good.

questions.stem_md: As incomes rose in an imagined Bihar village, families bought less coarse grain and more fine rice. The income elasticity of demand for coarse grain is

options.text_md: positive and greater than one
positive and less than one
zero
negative

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** negative. Demand falls as income rises, so income elasticity is negative: coarse grain is an inferior good for these families.

questions.stem_md: When the fare of app-based cabs rose in an imagined Bengaluru suburb, the number of auto-rickshaw rides increased. The cross elasticity of demand for auto rides with respect to cab fares is

options.text_md: negative, because the two are complements
positive, because the two are substitutes
zero, because they are unrelated
equal to the price elasticity of cabs

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** positive, because the two are substitutes. A rise in the price of cabs raised the demand for autos: the variables move together, so cross elasticity is positive and the goods are substitutes.

questions.stem_md: After the price of printers rose sharply at an imagined Nagpur electronics market, sales of printer ink cartridges fell. The cross elasticity of demand for cartridges with respect to printer prices is

options.text_md: negative, showing that the goods are complements
positive, showing that the goods are substitutes
zero, showing that the goods are unrelated
positive, showing that cartridges are inferior goods

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** negative, showing that the goods are complements. A higher printer price reduced cartridge demand: opposite directions give a negative cross elasticity, which marks complements.

questions.stem_md: For families in an imagined Pune suburb, arrange these goods from the lowest to the highest likely income elasticity of demand.

options.text_md: Foreign holidays (luxury: positive, greater than one)
Cheap coarse grain (inferior good: negative)
Milk (necessity: positive, less than one)
Salt (necessity: positive but close to zero)

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). Inferior goods have negative income elasticity, necessities between zero and one (salt nearest zero), and luxuries above one.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The cross elasticity of demand between two complementary goods is positive.

**Reason (R):** Complementary goods are goods that can be used in place of each other.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are false: complements have a negative cross elasticity (a dearer printer reduces ink demand), and goods used in place of each other are substitutes, not complements.

questions.stem_md: What does the sign and size of income elasticity of demand tell us about a good? Explain with the three cases.
questions.solution_md: Three cases with interpretation.

answer.model_answer_md: **Negative:** demand falls as income rises — an **inferior** good. **Positive but less than one:** demand rises less than proportionately — a **necessity**. **Positive and greater than one:** demand rises more than proportionately — a **luxury**.

questions.stem_md: For an imagined Guwahati household, state the likely sign of cross elasticity of demand in each pair and give the reason: (a) tea and coffee, (b) cars and petrol, (c) umbrellas and school bags.
questions.solution_md: Sign plus relationship for each pair.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) **Positive:** tea and coffee are **substitutes**; a dearer coffee raises the demand for tea. (b) **Negative:** cars and petrol are **complements**; dearer petrol lowers the demand for cars. (c) **Zero:** umbrellas and school bags are **unrelated**, so a change in the price of one does not affect demand for the other.

questions.stem_md: A retail chain plans new stores in an imagined fast-growing town where incomes are rising quickly. Advise it which kinds of goods to stock more of, using the idea of income elasticity of demand.
questions.solution_md: Three categories with stocking advice.

answer.model_answer_md: Goods with **high positive income elasticity** (luxuries such as branded clothes, electronics, eating out) will see demand **grow faster than incomes**, so the chain should expand them. **Necessities** with low positive elasticity grow slowly, so keep steady stocks. **Inferior goods** with **negative** income elasticity will see falling demand, so it should **reduce** them as the town grows richer.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [2 + 3]

(a) Distinguish between price elasticity, income elasticity and cross elasticity of demand.
(b) Explain how the signs of income elasticity and cross elasticity help a business in an imagined Indian city to classify the goods it sells.
questions.solution_md: Three definitions; signs and their business use.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Price elasticity** measures the response of quantity demanded to the good's **own price**; **income elasticity** measures the response to **consumers' income**; **cross elasticity** measures the response to the **price of a related good**.
(b) A **positive income elasticity** marks a **normal good** (greater than one a **luxury**, less than one a **necessity**); a **negative** one marks an **inferior good**. A **positive cross elasticity** marks **substitutes**, a **negative** one **complements**, and **zero** unrelated goods. The business can expect luxuries to grow as incomes rise, watch rival substitutes' prices, and price complements together.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [2 + 3]

(a) Explain the total expenditure (outlay) method of judging price elasticity of demand.
(b) A farmers' group in an imagined Nashik district wants to raise its onion income by selling less and charging more. Using the outlay method, evaluate when this plan works.
questions.solution_md: Method in three cases; condition of inelastic demand and its limits.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Compare buyers' **total spending** before and after a price change. If spending moves **opposite** to price, demand is **elastic**; if it is **unchanged**, demand is **unitary**; if it moves in the **same direction** as price, demand is **inelastic**. It shows the degree but not an exact value.
(b) The plan works only if demand for their onions is **inelastic**: then a higher price with smaller sales still **raises total spending** on onions, and so their income. If buyers have **close substitutes**, such as onions from other districts, demand for **this group's** onions is **elastic**, and spending would **fall**. So the group must act together and supply a large share of the market.

marking_scheme.step: (a) three cases of the outlay method

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about two imagined traders in a Lucknow market. [2 + 2]

(i) A chikan kurta seller cut her price from ₹800 to ₹720, and weekly sales rose from 50 to 60 kurtas. A lemon seller cut his price from ₹100 to ₹90 a kg, and sales rose from 200 to 206 kg. Calculate the price elasticity of demand for each.
(ii) Give one reason each for the difference in their elasticities.
questions.solution_md: Two percentage-method results, then factors.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Kurtas: quantity rises **10 ÷ 50 = 20 per cent**, price falls **80 ÷ 800 = 10 per cent**, so **Ed = 2**. Lemons: quantity rises **6 ÷ 200 = 3 per cent**, price falls **10 ÷ 100 = 10 per cent**, so **Ed = 0.3**.
(ii) Kurtas are a **semi-luxury** with many **substitutes** (other designs and shops), so buyers respond strongly. Lemons are a cheap **daily necessity** taking a **tiny share of income**, so buyers hardly change their purchases.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [2 + 2]

(i) A city bus service in an imagined Kanpur finds that when it raised fares, its total collection fell. What does this indicate about the elasticity of demand for its rides? Explain.
(ii) Suggest, with a reason, one change the service could make to its fares, and describe the diagram that shows demand of this kind.
questions.solution_md: Outlay method conclusion; fare advice and flat-curve diagram.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The fare **rose** and total collection **fell**: spending moved **opposite** to price, so by the outlay method demand for the rides is **elastic (Ed > 1)**; riders switched to autos, cycles or walking.
(ii) The service should **lower fares** (or roll back the rise): with elastic demand, a lower fare raises ridership more than proportionately and so **raises collection**. Diagram: a **relatively flat** downward-sloping demand curve, with quantity on the x-axis and fare on the y-axis.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [2 + 2]

(i) State the point method of measuring price elasticity on a straight-line demand curve and name the point where Ed = 1.
(ii) Explain how the method is applied to a curved demand curve.
questions.solution_md: Point method on a line; tangent method on a curve.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Price elasticity at a point = **lower segment ÷ upper segment**, the lower segment running from the point to the **quantity axis** and the upper segment to the **price axis**. At the **mid-point** the two are equal, so **Ed = 1**.
(ii) For a curve, draw a **tangent** that touches the curve at the point and extend it to both axes. Elasticity is then the **lower segment of the tangent** divided by its **upper segment**, measured from the point of contact.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) An imagined Jaipur auto-rickshaw union raised fares from ₹60 to ₹66 a ride, and weekly rides fell from 1,200 to 1,020. Calculate the price elasticity of demand by the percentage method and classify it.
(ii) Explain how the same conclusion can be reached by the total expenditure method, and state one advantage of the percentage method over it.
questions.solution_md: Percentage method calculation; outlay method reasoning; advantage.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Quantity falls **180 ÷ 1200 × 100 = 15 per cent**; price rises **6 ÷ 60 × 100 = 10 per cent**; **Ed = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5** after dropping the minus sign. As Ed is **greater than one**, demand for the rides is **relatively elastic**: riders respond more than in proportion to the fare.
(ii) By the **outlay method** we compare riders' **total spending**: with a higher fare and proportionately fewer rides, spending **falls** as the price **rises**. Spending moving **opposite** to price marks **elastic** demand, the same conclusion. The percentage method is better because it gives an **exact coefficient** (1.5), which allows comparison between goods and forecasts of revenue, while the outlay method only gives the **direction** (elastic, unitary or inelastic).

marking_scheme.step: Outlay method: spending falls as fare rises

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Explain any four factors that make the demand for a good elastic or inelastic, with an imagined Indian example of each.
(ii) A state government in an imagined coastal state wants to raise more revenue by taxing goods whose consumption will not fall much. Using price and income elasticity, evaluate which kinds of goods it should choose and the risks involved.
questions.solution_md: Four factors; tax choice by elasticity with risks.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Substitutes:** close substitutes make demand **elastic** — one brand of shampoo. **Nature:** **necessities** such as salt are **inelastic**, luxuries such as cruise tickets **elastic**. **Share of income:** goods taking a tiny share, such as matchboxes, are **inelastic**. **Time:** demand grows more **elastic in the long run**, as when commuters slowly move from petrol to the metro.
(ii) A tax raises price; revenue holds up only if quantity does not fall much, so the state should tax goods with **inelastic price demand**: necessities with few substitutes, or habit-forming goods. But taxing **necessities** with **low income elasticity** falls most heavily on **poor households**, which spend a larger share of income on them. Taxing luxuries with **high income elasticity** is fairer but their demand is more **elastic**, so revenue is less certain. The state must balance **revenue** against **equity**.

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined case about a Chennai tiffin centre and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined business and figures, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Quantity rises 60 ÷ 200 = 30 per cent; price falls 8 ÷ 40 = 20 per cent; Ed = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5.

**(b)** Substitutes make demand elastic.

**(c) (i)** Spending moved opposite to price.

**OR (c) (ii)** Flat curve for Ed > 1.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **1.5**

**(b)** The **availability of substitutes**: the canteen is a close substitute, so buyers move between them as relative prices change.

**(c) (i)** The price **fell** and the money buyers spent with her **rose** (her cash box was fuller): spending moved **opposite** to price, which by the outlay method marks **elastic** demand.

**OR (c) (ii)** A **relatively flat** downward-sloping curve: quantity changes **proportionately more** than price (Ed > 1), so a small fall in price brings a large move along the quantity axis.

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined report from a market town in Odisha and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Time and substitutes.

**(b)** Demand falls as income rises.

**(c) (i)** Negative cross elasticity, complements.

**OR (c) (ii)** Necessity, no substitute, no postponement.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **time period**: in the long run a **substitute** (solar lanterns) became available, so demand became more **elastic**.

**(b)** **Negative**: they buy less as income rises, so broken rice is an **inferior good** for them.

**(c) (i)** A **fall** in the price of phones **raised** the demand for covers: the variables move in **opposite** directions, so cross elasticity is **negative**, showing the goods are **complements**.

**OR (c) (ii)** Kerosene was a **necessity** for light with **no substitute** at first, and buying could **not be postponed**; so a higher price barely reduced the quantity bought.
